posts.body_html:
Hi, is the sulphur method still going well? I am also trying it now because I don't like to use chemical systemic fungicides because they are quite toxic. Moreover, fungi quickly become resistant to them. Growing plants with regular applications of toxic chemicals feels like being a doctor having to keep cancer patients alive with chemotherapy. I am growing Disa in transparant pots in living sphagnum. Does the sulphur affect the sphagnum? Sulphur increases acidity and repels aphids, and is therefore beneficial to Disa in other ways too. I leave my Disa outside in the rain all year here in the Netherlands and had no problems with rot until this summer, probably due to repotting stress (the sphagnum had died in a few pots) and heat, but I only grow them for one and a half years.

posts.body_html:
Good question Peter! My disa collection crashed very hard last year: the plants produced the biggest tubers I've ever seen, and after they were transplanted, one by one, they all rotted out!

No amount of sulfur will save plants that become vulnerable after a heat stress event. I THINK my mistake last year was assuming that the plants would be okay under 70% shade cloth during a heat wave. Unfortunately, I suspect the soil temperature rose too high for too many days in a row, and even though we had cool nights, it wasn't enough. They received ZERO fertilizer for several months prior to rotting and are watered with only Deionized water, so that rules out nutrients being the cause of rot.

That said, if you only have a few fungal spots here and there and the plants were not previously exposed to any intensely stressful weather events, sulfur will absolutely work, so long as the environment stays ideal for the plants. What are ideal conditions?
1) cool but not freezing temperatures
2) bright, indirect light
3) moderate humidity
4) low TDS in the soil

I've found that luke cold-ish temperatures (between 19C and 25C) coupled with high humidity without significant drops in temperature at night can also cause fungal outbreaks. This usually happens here in CA when we have the the tail end of tropical storms dumping rain here. If the plants get wet, it'll be a disaster.

In a greenhouse, everything can be controlled, so that is the ultimate way to keep them alive long term. Outdoors, you really have to be on top of your game ALL the time to keep them alive past several years. Bottom watering also helps, try not to get the leaves wet when it's humid outside. When there is low humidity, it's totally fine!

This is a new batch of plants, the ones that died off last year looked just like this prior to dying off!




Out of over a hundred plants, less than a dozen survived the rot! Here's one survivor:


After growing these plants for decades, the lesson learned is that if you grow outdoors, you're at the mercy of the weather, and must adapt when it becomes unfavorable for the plants. Right after a stressful weather event, the plants usually look completely normal and fine, but a few weeks to even a month later, they may all crash all of the sudden and leave you wondering what happened!

My Disas just survived being exposed to 112F (44C) for a few days, and the nights went down int the 60's (16C or so) More importantly, the soil temperature remains cool during the heat waves. This time, the plants were moved into 100% shade to make sure they stay cool. In a few weeks, we will be able to support or refute the hypothesis that high soil temperatures was the root cause of the rot issue last year!

posts.body_html:
Thanks Meizzwang. The climate here on the coast of the Netherlands is different than yours. The last couple of years we are having wet and mild autumns and winters, and dry and warm summers with a few short heatwaves of up to 35c. Spring is becoming more dry and cool. A few days ago the autumn rains set in, bringing a sudden end to summer. What I noticed so far about my Disas is that they like rainy cool weather. Summer is the dangerous time, and I will not repot again in summer. Like you, Disa with large tubers rotted away after repotting. I am not sure whether it was just the weather. The reason why I repotted them is because the sphagnum had died and the Disa didn't look happy. And I repotted them in dead sphagnum instead of green living sphagnum. And perhaps they received too much sunlight. Probably a combination of unfavorable things. Many of my Pleione orchids died due to stem rot during early summer. Probably due to high humidity. I have an open unheated greenhouse but I only put the Disa in there during night frosts. A greenhouse especially dedicated to them is not possible now. Trichoderma is another biofungicide that I am experimenting with. Although I am not sure whether it will work on Disa in living sphagnum, it will do no harm, and the auxins might benefit the growth of Disa. If it works, it should protect the tubers against rot.
Your remaining plants look happy and healthy. You will have a lot of work dividing and repotting them.

Sept 19, 2022 14:37:42 GMT -5 meizzwang said:
I just know that growing Disas outside isn't easy, no matter how experienced you are! I think there's more success long term if you can control the environmental all year round, like in a greenhouse.
The German lady I got my Disa from grows them outdoors in living sphagnum in transparent plastic pots since 2016. She wrote me ''I have them without shade south- east - south outside to 0 degrees Celsius. More UV gives better colors, shading from Mai at the heat of midday . They love sun, wind and coolness by the roots.'' She occasionally gives a seaweed based fertilizer as a foliar fertilizer. Another lady here in the Netherlands grows them on her balcony. But the conditions and ways of all growers are different and what works for one might not work for the other. Here pictures of the German plants. My pots with surviving plants look similar.

had a few disas flower in late November/early december! I guess their photoperiods got messed up by us turning on the lights at night? No clue what happened, these should be somewhat dormant right now! Pics taken 11/27/22:




Several other plants produced flower buds in November, and I picked them out, hoping that this would save energy and allow the plant to grow back, but it looks like it didn't work. In some cases, the plant looks like it's totally dead after producing flower buds, probably because they didn't form tubers. Everything that didn't flower is in good shape:
